messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Detective
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 63

At nineteen, he is one of the youngest detectives in his unit, and before the kidnapping he carries that fact with a mix of pride and pressure. He likes the clean logic of police work, the feeling that careful attention can bring order to fear. He works long hours and tells his girlfriend that he does not mind; he wants to prove himself. He is alert, serious for his age, and already used to being underestimated until he starts talking through a case.

The event that changes him begins as an assignment he believes is routine surveillance. He and a senior officer are following up on a lead connected to a robbery crew. He remembers the street first: narrow, noisy, lined with small shops, nothing that seems remarkable. Then everything narrows quickly. Men come from both sides, weapons appear, and he understands too late that they have been expected. He is hit hard across the head and shoved into the back of a vehicle. He tries to memorize turns, count seconds, listen for landmarks like he has been trained to do, but panic keeps breaking his concentration. He thinks, with humiliating clarity, that he is going to die before he has even become the kind of officer he has wanted to be.

They keep him captive for several days in a locked room. He does not know exactly how many because the room has no window and light comes and goes at someone else’s choosing. He is tied for long stretches, questioned, threatened, slapped awake when he drifts off. Sometimes they want information; sometimes they seem to want only to watch him fear them. The worst part, when he tells it now, is not even the pain but the helplessness. He hears footsteps outside the door and his whole body stiffens. He studies voices, tries to guess moods, learns to keep his face blank. At one point he hears another person crying in a nearby room and cannot do anything. He still feels ashamed when he remembers that he stays silent, focused only on surviving the next hour.

When he is eventually found during a police operation, he comes out into daylight squinting, disoriented, and furious at how relieved he feels. In the first days afterward, everyone around him speaks in urgent, practical terms—statements, debriefing, medical checks, congratulations that he is alive. He goes along with it. He tells the story in flat pieces and notices that people seem reassured by how calm he sounds. Inside, though, he feels as if his body has not understood that the room is gone.

Back at home, sleep becomes the place where captivity continues. He wakes drenched in sweat, already halfway off the bed, sometimes swinging before he is fully conscious. In dreams, the door opens and he cannot move; in others, he is back in the vehicle counting turns that never end. He begins sleeping with the light on, then with the television running, then hardly sleeping at all. During the day he startles at footsteps in hallways and at doors closing somewhere behind him. If someone walks too close on the street, his chest tightens and he has to fight the urge to spin around.

He returns to work sooner than his girlfriend and mother think he should. He tells them staying home would be worse. At the station he throws himself into tasks that let him feel competent: reviewing footage, organizing reports, following timelines. But fieldwork is different now. Every unknown building feels charged. He scans exits before he hears what anyone is saying. In interviews, if a suspect leans forward suddenly, he loses the thread of the conversation. He hates that his mind can be hijacked so easily. Because he is a detective, people assume he can handle details of violence; instead he finds himself caught by sensory fragments—the scrape of a chair, the smell of damp concrete, a key turning in a lock.

His girlfriend notices the changes before he can admit them. He no longer likes enclosed spaces, avoids crowded minibuses, and insists on sitting near doors in restaurants. When she reaches for him unexpectedly, he flinches and then looks wounded by his own reaction. He stops answering her calls on difficult days because he does not know how to explain the mixture of anger, fear, and numbness he carries around. Sometimes he wants her close enough to prove he is still here; sometimes her concern makes him feel trapped, and he withdraws without warning. They argue about small things that are not small things.

He tells himself he should be grateful, stronger, over it by now. Instead he moves through the present as if part of him is still listening outside a locked door. He trusts his instincts less, yet cannot turn them off. The world that once felt readable through careful observation now feels full of hidden intentions. He keeps going to work, keeps trying to act like the same young detective he was before, but he lives with the constant sense that danger is not past—it is merely waiting for the next moment he lets his guard down.
